So I said to myself: "If a vote is taken on the Van den Bos report, vote in favour - remember that, Fatuzzo - but also point out that it would be appropriate to pay attention to and check that the aid granted to the population of Bangladesh under this agreement is also used to enable the state to grant a pension to some elderly people."

It clearly emerges in whose favour the "bottlenecks in infrastructure", particularly in "transport and energy infrastructure", are to be eliminated, the "financial system made efficient" or "transparent and democratic institutional framework conditions" created, an euphemism with which one addresses all the impairments to Western investors in view of the omnipresent corruption.

Under these circumstances, the proposed provision of EU funds essentially serves to compensate for the state's failure in this country and to shift the costs of the infrastructure needed by the large corporations to the European institutions, in order to enable the latter to extract the maximum possible profit from one of the poorest populations in the world.

Since swift intervention by police forces is just as much a continuation of politics by other means as war, and since we no longer trust the policy of the European Union more than that of the member states, we are opposed to any form of military or police intervention by the European Union, wherever it may be.

As for the desire to waive geographical restrictions for this rapid intervention force, this is reminiscent of the raids of former colonial powers in Africa and elsewhere, such as those committed by France to protect dictators rejected by the people, or as currently being carried out by Great Britain in Sierra Leone.

The proposal for a regulation to create the special facility for crisis management is nothing other than the framework for non-military, yet nonetheless imperialist, political and economic interventions in any part of the world. What the leading EU circles are striving for is a mechanism for the immediate mobilization of human and financial resources that can be rapidly deployed, not only in "crisis situations" (perhaps the authors of the text could tell us once what characteristics define a "crisis situation"), but also when merely a threat or even just an impairment of the so-called support and cooperation programs with these countries is to be feared.

The initial impression was further reinforced, among other things, by the formulation of the triggers for the special facility: Although it was outlined with high goals, it does not reveal what it practically consists of, whereas it would have been sufficient, while maintaining the regular intervention areas provided for by the Community regulations, to point out those that, mindful of the need for speed, would set the reaction instrument in motion.

Finally, objections could be raised against the hesitant information of the European Parliament, which is also due to the fact that only the consultation procedure was provided for; nevertheless, driven by the desire for a future extension of the co-decision procedure, I am of the opinion that the Commission, in the face of special cases with geographical significance and obvious political character, cannot avoid immediately informing the European Parliament.

Despite numerous statements by the European Parliament in favour of harmonising social and tax legislation, and despite concrete proposals by the Commission to update and simplify Regulation 1408/71, it is the ministers of the Member States themselves who are blocking this necessary reform process in the Council of Ministers and preventing the realisation of the internal market for persons.

The report on the situation of cross-border workers, which our Committee on Employment and Social Affairs has presented to us, is certainly based on the laudable intention of not discriminating against cross-border workers in terms of their pay and working conditions and their social security, and of resolving any remaining problems in this regard.

If the guidelines on the conservation of natural habitats, the elimination of PCB and PCT, and the protection of waters against pollution by nitrates are not sufficiently applied in the Member States, this does not mean that these guidelines are bad and need to be amended, as some people in this House would have us believe.

The Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, must on the one hand be uncompromising towards the Member States to ensure that they comply with the guidelines, and on the other hand must resist attempts to amend these texts before they have been able to demonstrate their full usefulness, particularly in the areas of water pollution by nitrates and the protection and enhancement of particularly valuable natural areas.

Agriculture and rural areas are indeed in decline, to which the common agricultural policy has made a significant contribution, as it promotes the concentration of areas, the intensification of production, and the increasing vertical organization of agricultural production, leading to the desolation and depopulation of rural regions, as evidenced by the decline in jobs and businesses by approximately 22% and 20% respectively since 1990.

What has been happening in most of our Member States since the rather hysterical escalation of this crisis is certainly not helping to motivate young people to stay in agriculture, and even less so to see their future in rural areas, where, as our report so aptly puts it, they have an important social function to fulfill by dedicating themselves to landscape conservation and maintenance and contributing to meeting the economic, social, and ecological needs of rural areas.

More than ever, we must be concerned about the future of agriculture in the European Union in the face of this crisis of confidence, which has been triggered particularly among consumers, where the number of farmers under 35 years of age has been declining the most for some time - by 28% - and the proportion of farmers is decreasing in almost all Member States.

We must also defend and secure the designations of origin of our quality products, including wine, in the World Trade Organization, because our future in the EU and with regard to exports to third countries lies in high-quality products for which there are solvent and discerning consumers both here and around the world.

I wholeheartedly endorse this report, as it encompasses and well-formulates everything that is right and important for the preservation and promotion of agricultural family businesses in Europe, a basic requirement for promoting ecological agriculture with high-quality, regionally typical products, which consumers must learn to appreciate and pay fairly for.

Mr President, the pensioners' party I represent in this European Parliament holds the view and makes the demand that the Commission, the European Parliament and the Council must change the fisheries policy in essential parts: This concerns the by now deeply ingrained habit of fishing in foreign waters and then calming one's conscience by paying a certain amount of money to the governments of the countries whose territorial waters we have fished.

Mr. President, I would like to express, first of all, on behalf of my group, that we explicitly welcome the continuation of a common fisheries policy within the European Union, because we are of the opinion that the management of resources is the best way to also ensure the social and economic development of many coastal regions of the European Union in the future, which, apart from their own natural resources, such as fishing and aquaculture, have no other advantages and no other employment and development opportunities.

Mr President, although I voted in favour of this report on the Common Fisheries Policy, I call on the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission to pay closer attention to and monitor a forgotten aspect under point 20 of the report, namely the way in which, and whether, pension amounts, levels and conditions in the fisheries sector, and in particular for retired fishermen in the artisanal fisheries sector, are controlled.

Since the Community, in accordance with the relevant declaration in Article 5(1) of Annex IX to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, is solely responsible for the conservation and management of fish stocks and is therefore empowered to lay down the corresponding rules and provisions, the Commission should make use of this power and establish the exclusive fishing right, also for Greek fishermen, at 12 nautical miles.

The Commission sets the following priorities: improved coherence between the various objectives pursued by the CFP, in particular between the conservation of resources, economic viability and job security in areas dependent on fishing; greater consideration of the economic dimension of the fisheries sector; improved integration of environmental and fisheries policies; improvement of management instruments, in particular the inclusion of multi-annual management objectives; a more transparent decision-making process and the preservation of the external dimension of the CFP.

Until 31 December 2002, we still have two years in which to think about and decide on a common policy. According to the European Commission's schedule, 18 questions arise in this context, such as free or non-free access to Community waters, control or management of the market for fisheries and aquaculture products, international fisheries agreements, scientific research activities concerning fish stocks, and the specific characteristics of the Mediterranean area.

The joint resolution on the "Balkan Syndrome" merely serves to whitewash the criminal policy of NATO and the European Union, which intervened in Yugoslavia under the pretext of wanting to defend human rights, thereby causing irreparable human and material damage.

The joint resolution denies the clear link between the use of depleted uranium and the occurrence of cancer and leukemia in soldiers who were involved in the occupation forces in Bosnia and Kosovo, but also in the Gulf War. It limits itself to the pious wish for "an open and transparent debate" as well as the establishment of a working group and calls on "the member states that are also members of NATO to propose a moratorium on the use of ammunition with depleted uranium...", while the EU is merely asked to "consider the use of other types of ammunition", i.e. it can continue to kill, but with "clean" weapons.

The European Parliament has naturally acted consistently towards itself, because - as the war criminal and former NATO Secretary General, now the EU's High Representative, Javier Solana, cynically pointed out in his speech - the European Parliament itself has persistently demanded military intervention in the Balkans, both in Bosnia and in Kosovo.

That the armies of the greatest powers have known for ten years about the harmfulness of ammunition with depleted uranium, even for those who use it, only proves that the general staffs show the same disregard for their own soldiers as for the civilian population and the opposing forces.

Since the beginning of the atomic age with World War II, the dangers and precautionary measures that must be observed when handling uranium and other radioactive substances have been well known, as it is a highly toxic (chemically and radiologically toxic) element that is also genetically hazardous if inhaled or ingested.

The use of this type of weapon by the United States and other NATO countries during the Gulf War, in Bosnia, and in Kosovo has already caused the death of many soldiers, suffering and fatalities among the inhabitants of the bombed areas, and the contamination of the environment in the affected regions.

In view of the extent of the crime against entire civilian populations, it is urgently necessary to identify the main perpetrators of these criminal acts against humanity, to establish their guilt and to condemn them, as well as to immediately prohibit the production, testing, use and sale of weapons with depleted uranium and not just adopt a moratorium.

We all know that these weapons, which were used by NATO in the Gulf War (1991), in Bosnia (1994-95), and in Kosovo (1999), had severe consequences initially for the bombed civilian population, but also for the environment and the military personnel of NATO, the Iraqi, Bosnian, Serbian, and Kosovar forces.

Mr President, following all the tragic events connected with the bombing of Yugoslavia and the revelations about the use of ammunition with depleted uranium, it is now urgently necessary to ban this type of weapon, which even after use still has dangerous effects over a long period and strikes blindly, i.e. without distinction, all those who risk coming into contact with them.

It is equally important and urgent to conceive a comprehensive policy of assistance, prevention, and rehabilitation for all areas in Yugoslavia that are suffering from the consequences of the use of these munitions, in order to protect public health and the environment, rehabilitate soils and waters, and ensure the steady economic development of the country and the entire region.

Apart from that, the resolution proposal briefly addresses extremely serious questions related to the analysis and necessary research of depleted uranium, but does not address anywhere the continued efforts to conceal and hide facts, independent, well-known research works, even scientific papers from NATO countries that prove the dangers of depleted uranium and name precautionary measures that these countries impose on their armed forces.

In conclusion, I would like to express my bewilderment at the political about-face that has emerged during our discussion. While some people previously accused us that our criticism of Milosevic's policy served the interests of NATO and its bombing campaigns, Mr. Solana now accuses us of forgetting the human rights of the victims of Milosevic due to our reservations regarding depleted uranium.

The goal of the presidency of the council before this year's session is to unite the EU behind closed positions, to call on the candidate countries to participate in the EU's statements and resolutions, and to obtain the broadest possible support for the applications - this year, this particularly concerns the situation in Iran and Chechnya.

Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen. On behalf of my colleague, Mr. Patten, who has already departed for Moscow, I would like to congratulate the Parliament on today's debate, as it offers us a valuable opportunity to exchange views on the forthcoming session of the UN Commission on Human Rights in Geneva.

I also observed with concern last year that the current Russian leadership - which includes many former KGB employees appointed by President Putin, who was himself a former KGB colonel - has shown great zeal in arresting so-called British, American, and Russian spies.

For this reason, the Council and the Member States must work towards the universal ratification of the key human rights instruments available to all countries. These include, in particular, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the aforementioned Convention on the Rights of the Child, the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, and the highly important Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment.

We also call on the EU to support the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and other international organisations and NGOs in the fight against the suppression of independent media - a point Lord Bethell has already raised - and journalists and writers, and to urge all states to abolish censorship, protect the right of access to official information, and lift restrictions on access to modern information technology, which is often the salvation for oppressed people.

Mr President, Mr Vitorino, Mr President-in-Office, when we are to take a decision on a subject such as human rights, we have two options: we can name principles and refrain from naming areas, or we can proceed as we have done, namely name areas and run the risk of forgetting some.

I fear that this year, too, my party, the Radical Party, will unfortunately again be among the few who, along with Wei Jinsheng and a few others, will defend human rights in China and Tibet, who will forcefully address the Chechnya issue, while the Council and the Union it represents will once again fail to make an appearance at the UN.

I say this in light of the genocide in Rwanda in 1994, where the international community had to watch as hundreds of thousands of people were murdered. With regard to Central Africa, I would like to urge the European Union to take more energetic action and the United Nations to show greater vigilance.

With regard to the developing countries, we are therefore forced to develop a special strategy for the sanctions, so that not only those are affected whom we actually wanted to help and who already had to suffer beforehand.

Of course, Mr. President, I concur with the criticism of China regarding Tibet, of Russia regarding Chechnya, the criticism of human rights abuses in the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians, as well as the criticism of this repulsive public execution that took place.

For example, Sweden has for many years been responsible for a resolution on the situation in Burma/Myanmar at the UN General Assembly, and the Union as a whole is actively engaged in discussions within the International Labour Organization, ILO, in view of the fact that forced labour still exists in Burma.

(Applause) Secondly: We urge you to set up a conference, fairly quickly - the preparations must begin under your presidency and should then lead to a decision in Laeken under Belgian presidency - which is based on the methodology and the model of the Convention, with strong participation of the European Parliament and, of course, the national governments, but above all also the Commission.

There is another typo: the Czech Republic and Hungary, which have the same population as Belgium and Portugal, are supposed to have only 20 MEPs, the other two countries 22. Let's also give the Czech Republic and Hungary 22 MEPs in the European Parliament and not start the expansion with discrimination against these two countries!

We are deeply concerned to see that, also due to the actions of the General Secretariat of the Council - and Mr Solana, whom I hold in high esteem, is indeed more concerned with the task of the High Representative - at the head of the General Secretariat of the Council, there are certain barriers, in that one is unwilling to provide either the Commission or the European Parliament with information.

Sweden is taking over the presidency of the Council for the first time and has set its priorities, the famous three "E"s, which are in line with the manifesto of European socialists and social democrats, because I can proudly say that Mr Persson and his party belong to my political family, and the Prime Minister of Sweden has also made a defence of the European social model and its adaptability in times of globalisation, which fills us with pride.

The next topic that will occupy the Swedish Presidency and all of us from the year 2001, which has just begun, until 2004 - that is four years with many elections, including the European ones - is the topic "Post-Nice".

I would like to call on the Council to participate in this first phase, which you are launching and which must be concluded in Laeken, in which we must find the method to move forward and not just talk about the future of the Union, but to examine what the future of the enlarged Union will be, because after Nice, these countries are already among us and must learn how we function, which is a rather complicated topic.

I look forward to the answers to my three questions: about the possibility of changing the discrimination against Hungary and the Czech Republic in the Treaty of Nice, what you will undertake to introduce the Tobin tax, and how you stand on Turkey's participation in the EU military and its influence on it.

If you, Mr President, were to show some compassion and persuade your colleagues in the Council to bring this conference forward to 2003 or postpone it to 2005, perhaps the honour of this Parliament, which often does not know exactly what this word means, would be saved.

Madam President, Mr. President of the Council, Mr. President of the Commission, esteemed colleagues! Although I am coincidentally wearing a Nice tie today, I still cannot help but note that, just as in Amsterdam, we had to experience once again in Nice that the Intergovernmental Conference as an instrument has reached its limits.

In a first phase, a discussion and opinion-forming process at the level of national parliaments should take place in parallel to the discussion initiated under the Swedish presidency, and at the invitation of the European Council - and as soon as possible - which, like the European Parliament, would have to submit a proposal regarding this division of competences by around spring 2002.

Only on this basis should a convention be convened with the participation of constitutional experts, European law experts, representatives of national parliaments, the European Parliament, national governments, but also the governments of the accession countries and, of course, the Court of Justice and civil society, and be tasked with drawing up a proposal for a catalogue, roughly by spring 2003.

As representatives of the peoples and regions, we see Sweden as an ally in defending values that are important to us, including linguistic and cultural diversity. However, when you speak of a stronger involvement of national parliaments, we want the institutions of our constitutionally recognized regions, our regional governments, to receive the same attention.

On the issue of expansion, we do not see the most important thing merely in the adoption of the material community acquis, but demand that the focus be placed on the ethical acquis communautaire, i.e. on democracy, respect for human rights and minorities first and foremost, so that Europe can truly represent a community of values, in short, a community.

That is why the offer to participate that you have submitted to this Parliament today reassures us, especially in view of your statements, to which Mr Poettering referred shortly beforehand and which apparently implied that the Commission was an institution suffering from a major democratic deficit, and that this Parliament should be dissolved after the 1999 elections and the low voter turnout of the citizens of your country.

Firstly, the Swedish Presidency of the Council will convene a Council meeting or a special session to which the government representatives of the acceding countries will be invited, on the one hand to move the negotiations forward and on the other hand to send the important signal to the public that enlargement is not just a political goal, a mirage, a goal still far away, but that we are actually making the necessary progress?

Like some other speakers today, I am also concerned about the tendency to often and emphatically emphasize the inter-state model at the expense of the so-called Community Approach, which assigns a stronger role and significance to the Commission.

If you succeed in convincing your fellow citizens that the euro is a good project, that it is stable internally, that its external stability is also constantly improving, if you can convince them to support this major work of European integration, you will also contribute to this area of the European Union being better understood by its citizens.

The decision I have already mentioned states that a citizen of an EU member state who seeks consular assistance from a diplomatic or consular mission of another member state is to be treated as if he were a citizen of the country represented by the embassy or consulate in question.

At the same time, the Council of Europe announces that torture is still a daily occurrence in Turkish police stations, and Amnesty International condemns the torture, the impunity of those responsible, and the general human rights violations by Turkey, and calls on the European Union to demand that torture be stopped immediately, and not just in 2002-2003, as provided for in the procedure for Turkey's accession to the European Union.

I would like to ask the President of the Council the following: In the light of the tragedy that we have witnessed and that has officially cost the lives of at least 60 people, and in view of the torture, the fate of people who may be in prison simply because they spoke their mother tongue, and the hunger strike in which around 200 prisoners are still involved, will the Swedish Presidency take any public initiative, will it demand explanations and commitments from the Turkish Government? And will the Swedish Presidency finally take action for the release of the Member, Leyla Zana, who was awarded the Sakharov Prize by this Parliament?

I would, however, like to ask a few more in-depth questions: I am concerned about the de facto existing political union between Belarus and Poland, as well as the question of to what extent the Swedish Presidency of the Council is willing to also exert pressure on Russia, which is also part of a political union with Belarus. To what extent does it recognize the consequences for democracy and Russia's position in the international community that arise from the union with a country that can hardly be described as a democracy?

As for the UN Commission based in Geneva, which has been dealing with settling claims arising from the Gulf War since its end, I think it would be wise to wait for a UN investigation into the continuation of this Commission's work before the Union takes a position.

The Union, inter alia, made it clear at the last ASEAN Ministerial Meeting in Vientiane in December 2000 that it expects the EU Troika to have the same opportunities for contact with all parties involved, whether they be representatives of the government, the National League for Democracy or ethnic minorities.

The Council also welcomes the fact that the EU and ASEAN, in their joint declaration adopted in Vientiane, undertook to support the efforts of the UN Secretary-General's Special Envoy for Burma, Tan Sri Razali Ismail, towards a positive development in Burma.

In conclusion, one final critical remark: in 1994, Aung San Suu Kyi held talks with the SLORC, as the SPDC was called at the time, and she was accused of being too inflexible and that it was impossible to work with her because she refused to deviate from her demand for the SLORC to recognize the 1990 elections.

Concerning: Fisheries and Swedish Presidency Can the Council, under the Swedish Presidency, explain the level of importance it attaches to the fisheries sector, taking into account the extremely difficult situation in which fishermen in Ireland and other EU countries currently find themselves, and can it explain its priorities regarding the next development programme for the fishing fleet for the period 2002-2006?

In addition to the structural problems specifically addressed in the question, the problem areas given priority attention by the Council also include the start of work on the Commission's Green Paper on the future of the Common Fisheries Policy and the preparation of a proposal by the Presidency on fisheries and the environment, i.e. on integrating environmental issues and the principle of sustainable development into the Common Fisheries Policy.

Following the agenda is the report (A5-0393/2000) by Mr Simpson on behalf of the Committee on Regional Policy, Transport and Tourism on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulation (EEC) No 3922/91 of the Council on the harmonization of technical requirements and administrative procedures in civil aviation.

In the Committee on Regional Policy, Transport and Tourism, however, it is clear that the trade unions and the airlines are best suited to finding a solution to this problem, and so the members of the Committee have agreed on a compromise to give all parties until 1 May 2001 to reach an agreement on the basis of which the text of the new Section Q will then be drawn up.

That's why I also say very clearly: As much as we can agree with your report in many parts, we do not think it is appropriate for the parliament to establish its own detailed basis in certain areas - keyword "sole flight attendant" or the duration of employment, i.e. how long someone has already been active as a flight attendant - in this regulation.

Mr President, Mr Simpson, Commissioner! Having just watched the news, I had hoped - and it almost seemed that way - that we would be having a discussion on fox hunting, on which there will undoubtedly be a most lively debate in the British Parliament this evening.

Although we do not yet have complete and 100 percent secure findings on this, we at least recognize the seriousness of the situation and are asking ourselves whether we should not request the Commission, in this case, through an amendment proposal - otherwise we would choose a different path - to take certain measures in this area.

Mr President, Mr Simpson has indeed submitted an excellent report. I can claim this because I am probably one of the few who are not only politically but also technically familiar with this sector, as before I took up my duties as a Member of this Parliament, I had completed around 10,000 hours of flying as a member of a cockpit crew.

I would like to point out that safety is the top priority in air traffic, with the understanding that this safety is based on two factors: on the one hand, the technical factor, i.e. the equipment, aircraft, airports, radio navigation and air traffic control facilities, etc., and on the other hand, the extremely significant human factor, which, although not decisive, has a very high share in aircraft accidents.

I'm not speaking here as a union representative, but as an airline passenger who would really like to have, if not an absolute, then at least the greatest possible guarantee that excessive strain on the human factor, which can sometimes have fatal consequences, is avoided.

Either the parties agree by May, or we expect the Commission to make a proposal that we can incorporate into the second reading, because it is unacceptable that the crucial question for passenger safety, namely whether captains and crews are rested enough to perform their duties, is not regulated.

In conclusion, Mr President, I would like to stress the need to assist the Commission in its work in this highly complex field, the priority of establishing the European Aviation Safety Agency and the urgent need for an independent regulation on the issue of rest periods for crews, which we are currently addressing.

Based on this, the amendment we propose to the existing regulation has a twofold objective: on the one hand, it aims to further harmonise the regulatory system in the field of civil aviation safety by extending it to the harmonisation of operational requirements for aircraft; on the other hand, it is about establishing procedures that will enable the Community to process the variants and exemptions that Member States must apply from time to time for operational reasons.

Amendments 9 and 10 can be accepted unchanged, while amendments 6, 7, 8, and 11 would have to be revised in their wording, as we can now only accept them in principle and with revisions, just like amendments 12, 13, and 17.

With regard to the specific problem of thrombosis - which one of you mentioned - the Commission has written to the airlines asking them to inform passengers about the dangers, predisposing factors and the measures to minimize these risks, specifically in connection with thrombosis and general health problems.

Following the agenda is the report (A5-0381/2000) by Mrs Hedkvist Petersen on behalf of the Committee on Regional Policy, Transport and Tourism on the Commission's communication to the Council, the European Parliament, the Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions: Priorities for road safety in the EU - progress report and classification of measures.

Allow me, Commissioner, to briefly note the following: In my opinion, it is extremely impolite towards our parliament that, in anticipation of our discussion this evening, in which a regulation on the maximum permissible blood alcohol level is to be approved, the Commission member has now apparently already decided that a recommendation to the Member States would be sufficient.

Let us establish regulations, seek a greater degree of harmonisation, promote measures to make pedestrian and cycle traffic reasonable and safe, and seek formulas to reduce heavy goods traffic, at least in towns; let us harmonise speed limits through an ambitious legal framework, as proposed by the Commission in 1986, by rousing the Member States from their inertia.

In my opinion, this makes it clear that road safety cannot be sufficiently increased by isolated individual measures, but rather that this can only be achieved through a comprehensive package of measures, which includes traffic education, speed limits, alcohol limits, improved road construction, traffic guidance systems, a higher safety standard for vehicles, stricter controls on compliance with the road traffic regulations, and also a permanent inspection of vehicles in road traffic.

For this reason, I also deeply regret that the amendment to harmonize the re-registration of vehicles that have been involved in accidents within the European Union was not adopted, although independent expert opinions clearly prove a substantial link between vehicles that have been involved in accidents once and repeated involvement in accidents with increased fatal consequences.

And of course, we must also activate and more strongly involve local communities and regional authorities in matters of road traffic safety, in order to get closer to the citizens, while the information campaign must undoubtedly be continued with - if you will - more intelligent methods to reach the public and especially young people.

What is the point of lamenting that 95% of traffic accidents occur on road traffic and thus only an extremely small part on rail and air traffic, if the policy of all governments consists of openly or de facto favoring the car over all other modes of transport for passenger or freight transport.

Mr President, road safety can and must be a priority both for Europe as a whole and for each individual country. That is why I also agree with Ms Hedkvist Petersen's proposal - and I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate her on her report - to draw up a strategic plan for road safety and set a number of strict but also realistic quantitative targets.

Furthermore, other proposals mentioned in the report, such as stronger support for the European programme for the assessment of new vehicles, the promotion of campaigns in favour of the use of seatbelts, the development of telematics systems, and the mandatory installation of daytime running lights in motorcycles and vehicles, can be implemented relatively cost-effectively with high benefits for road traffic safety and public health.

On the one hand, no EU state would accept it if another member state were to tolerate a flight captain drinking alcohol in an airplane with 300 passengers, a ship's captain responsible for the safety of 1,000 people, or a train driver before taking responsibility for his passengers.

Information campaigns on best practices in EU states and mandatory measures to reduce accident causes such as alcohol, drug use, and medication intake, but also a guideline promoting the creativity of the automotive industry to expand safety tests or to promote the Euro-NCAP program for assessing new vehicles, can prove this.

Mr President, first and foremost, I would like to sincerely congratulate Ms Hedkvist Petersen on her comprehensive resolution on road safety, which demonstrates the European Parliament's interest - also evident in your speeches today - in an ambitious policy to combat the scourge of road accidents.

I would like to stress that I am in full agreement with the content of the report and its crowning glory, the resolution, both with regard to the current action programme, which is shortly to come to an end, and with regard to the future programme on road safety, the presentation of which the Commission has scheduled for the coming months.

In a first stage, the last priority measures defined within the framework of the current road safety programme must be implemented. In particular, it is proposed that the obligation to fit speed limiters be extended to a larger number of lorries by including vehicles with a lower payload.

In a second stage, a more systematic concept must be applied with a view to the future action program, by setting quantitative targets on a European scale. Their development must take place with the participation of the states in order to achieve greater effectiveness and complementarity between the measures defined by Brussels and those defined at national level.

Secondly, there are customs, habits, reasons that lead me to consider that this is the classic topic that should remain in the area of subsidiarity, and therefore we are only making a recommendation of 0.5. I assume that you hold a different view - I have already noticed this -, and it is also a fact that so far there has been no sufficient majority in the Council to launch such an initiative.

What I'm saying is that we haven't rejected the idea of developing regulations regarding front-end designs that are less hazardous for people, for unprotected bodies, but we simply want to be even more effective by gaining the support of the automotive sector.

Following the agenda is the report (A5-0358/2000) by Mrs Poli Bortone on behalf of the Committee on Regional Policy, Transport and Tourism on the Commission's communication to the European Parliament, the Council and the Economic and Social Committee on the implementation of the action programme set out in the communication on intermodality and intermodal freight transport in the European Union.

Analyzing the friction costs in intermodal freight transport in detail reveals that the main problem areas compared to traditional unimodal transport lie in higher prices, longer travel times, increasing average distances covered by the goods, reduced quality, greater risk of damage, restrictions on the type of goods transported, and more complex administrative procedures.

Ultimately, a series of obstacles caused by the lack of harmonization of deadlines and schedules between the individual modes of transport characterize the entire system, resulting in incompatibilities between the requirements associated with the goods transport chain and the operational requirements of the resources used in the process: For example, the working hours of drivers and crews are not coordinated with intermodal operations, and terminals cannot always adapt to train and ship schedules based on a 24-hour service.

In its report "Intermodality and Intermodal Freight Transport in the European Union", the Commission had outlined the objectives to be achieved in intermodal transport and divided them into three priority areas of intervention, so-called key actions, according to the specific problems. The first key action concerns the integration of infrastructure and modes of transport, the second interoperability and coordinated operation, and the third transport mode-independent services and regulations.
